title: Record New Evidence
content:
What problem does this solve?
A field record changes when new evidence arrives. You need to add an item to a list you already have, without building a brand-new list from scratch every time.

Basic syntax
  evidence.append("gray dust")

What actually happens
A list can be changed after you create it. append adds another element at the end of the same list. The name evidence still refers to that same list; it now has one more item.

When this is useful
Use append when something new should join a collection you already named — a recovered clue, a new party member, another entry in the log. Deeper list methods come later; this lesson focuses on append().
concepts: You can change a list after you create it
append adds an item at the end of the same list
After append, the name still refers to that same list

examples.title: Recovered evidence
examples.code:
evidence = ["broken lantern", "drag marks"]
evidence.append("gray dust")
print(evidence)
examples.explanation: append changes the list in place. evidence now holds three clues, ending with gray dust.

common_mistakes: Expecting append to return a new list — it changes the existing one and returns None
Replacing the whole list with a finished literal instead of adding to the list you already have

exercises.title: Predict the mutation
exercises.prompt: What does this print? Type the exact output, including square brackets and quotes.
exercises.code_to_predict:
evidence = ["broken lantern", "drag marks"]
evidence.append("torn cloak")
print(evidence)
hints: append adds to the end of the existing list.
print(evidence) shows the whole list, not just the new clue.
Python prints lists with square brackets and quotes around each string.

exercises.title: Add recovered evidence
exercises.prompt: evidence already has two clues. Append "gray dust" to that list, then print the list. Do not replace evidence with a brand-new three-item literal.
exercises.starter_code:
evidence = ["broken lantern", "drag marks"]
# Append gray dust, then print evidence
hints: Call a method on evidence to add one string at the end.
After adding, print the list variable itself.
Use evidence.append("gray dust"), then print evidence.

tests.name: evidence
tests.message: Add gray dust to the existing evidence list with append().

exercises.title: Report the new clue
exercises.prompt:
evidence already has two clues. Append "gray dust", then print exactly:
Newest evidence: gray dust

The clue in that line must come from indexing into the updated list and an f-string — do not hardcode gray dust only in the print.
exercises.starter_code:
evidence = ["broken lantern", "drag marks"]
# Append the new clue, then report it
hints: Append first so the new clue becomes the last item.
The last item of a three-element list is at index 2.
Print an f-string such as Newest evidence: {evidence[2]} after appending.

tests.name: evidence
tests.message: Append gray dust to evidence with append() before reporting it.
Use an f-string that reads from the evidence list.

tests.name: evidence
tests.message: Read the newest clue with evidence[...], not a hardcoded string alone.

exercises.success_message: Newest clue recorded. The list changed, and your report used its updated state.
